title: Eating well in the first trimester
summary: You do not need to eat for two yet. Focus on folate, small meals and foods you can keep down.
body: In the first three months your baby's brain, spine and organs are forming. You do not need much extra food yet, but the quality of what you eat matters a great deal.
Folate protects your baby's developing spine. Take the folic acid tablets given by your clinic every day, and add folate-rich foods such as gotukola, mukunuwenna, kankun, dhal, chickpeas and eggs.

If you feel sick, eat small amounts every two to three hours instead of three big meals. Dry foods such as crackers or plain roti before getting out of bed, ginger (inguru) tea and cold foods often help. Sip water through the day rather than drinking a lot at once.
Tell your PHM or clinic if you cannot keep any fluids down for a day, feel faint, or are losing weight. Severe sickness can be treated.

title: Iron-rich Sri Lankan foods for pregnancy
summary: Anaemia is common in pregnancy. Everyday foods, eaten the right way, can help your iron levels.
body: Your blood volume rises by almost half during pregnancy, so your body needs much more iron. Low iron can make you tired, breathless and pale, and can affect your baby's growth.
Good local sources include fish, lean meat, eggs, dhal, chickpeas, cowpea, green leaves such as mukunuwenna and kathurumurunga, and sprats (haal masso).
Iron from plants is absorbed better with vitamin C. Squeeze lime over your mallum, or eat guava, orange or amberella after your meal.

Tea and coffee block iron absorption. Try to leave about an hour between tea and your main meals or your iron tablet. Take calcium tablets at a different time from iron tablets, as your clinic advises.

title: Foods to avoid or limit while pregnant
summary: A short, practical list of the foods that are worth skipping or cutting down on until your baby arrives.
body: Avoid unripe and semi-ripe papaya. It contains latex that may trigger contractions. Fully ripe papaya in normal amounts is generally considered fine, but ask your doctor if you are unsure.
Cook eggs, meat and fish thoroughly, and choose boiled or pasteurised milk. Undercooked food can carry infections that are more harmful in pregnancy.
Large predatory fish such as shark and swordfish can contain mercury. Smaller fish such as salaya, hurulla and sprats are safer choices and give you healthy fats.

Keep caffeine under about 200 mg a day, which is roughly two cups of coffee or a few cups of plain tea. Avoid alcohol completely. Limit very salty foods such as dried fish, pickles and instant noodles, and very sweet foods such as kavum and sugary drinks.

title: Safe exercise during pregnancy
summary: Most women with a healthy pregnancy can stay active. Here is how to do it safely in Sri Lanka's heat.
body: If your pregnancy is uncomplicated, aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, for example 30 minutes of brisk walking on five days. You should still be able to talk while you move.

Walking, prenatal yoga, gentle stretching, swimming and pelvic floor exercises are good choices. Avoid contact sports, activities with a risk of falling and lying flat on your back for long periods after the first trimester.
Our weather is hot and humid. Exercise in the early morning or evening, wear loose cotton clothes and drink water before, during and after.
Stop and contact your doctor if you have bleeding, leaking fluid, chest pain, dizziness, a severe headache, calf pain or swelling, or regular painful tightenings.

title: Warning signs you should never ignore in pregnancy
summary: Know these signs. If you notice any of them, go to hospital or call 1990 straight away.
body: Go to hospital without waiting if you have vaginal bleeding, leaking fluid, a severe headache that does not go away, blurred vision or flashing lights, sudden swelling of your face or hands, or strong pain under your ribs.
A high fever, fits, difficulty breathing or regular contractions before 37 weeks also need urgent care.
If your baby is moving less than usual, do not wait until the next day to be checked.
Keep your pregnancy record, your clinic card and a phone with you. The Suwa Seriya ambulance service can be reached on 1990.

title: Getting to know your baby's movements
summary: Every baby has their own pattern. Learning it is one of the best ways to keep your baby safe.
body: Most mothers start to feel movements between 16 and 24 weeks. By the third trimester your baby will have a regular pattern of kicks, rolls and flutters.
Spend some time each day noticing when your baby is usually active. Many babies move more after meals or when you lie down.
Babies do not move less towards the end of pregnancy. If the movements slow down, stop or feel different from your baby's normal pattern, contact your hospital the same day.
Do not rely on home heartbeat monitors to reassure yourself. A proper check at the hospital is the safe choice.

title: Starting solid foods: your baby's first meals
summary: Breast milk alone is enough until six months. After that, here is how to add Sri Lankan family foods step by step.
body: Breast milk alone gives your baby everything they need for the first six months. At around six months, start other foods while continuing to breastfeed.

Begin with soft, smooth foods such as rice kanda, mashed pumpkin, carrot or potato, and mashed dhal. Introduce one new food at a time and wait a few days before the next, so you can notice any reaction.
Gradually add mashed fish, egg yolk and then whole egg, finely mashed green leaves and fruits such as banana and ripe papaya. Iron-rich foods are especially important from six months.
Do not add salt or sugar before your baby's first birthday, and do not give honey before one year. Your Child Health Development Record (CHDR) book has a feeding guide, and your PHM can help.

title: Feeding your toddler: a balanced Sri Lankan plate
summary: From one year, toddlers can share family meals. A few small changes make rice and curry perfect for them.
body: From about one year, your toddler can eat the same meals as the family, cut into small pieces and made less spicy. Take out their portion before adding lots of chilli or salt.
A good toddler plate has rice or another starch, a protein such as fish, egg, dhal or meat, a vegetable and a green leaf. Add a fruit as a snack.
Offer three meals and two small snacks a day. Good snacks include fruit, boiled chickpeas, curd, a boiled egg or a small piece of roti.
Avoid fizzy drinks, packaged juices and sweets as daily foods. Picky eating is normal. Keep offering a food many times without pressure.

title: Keeping little ones safe from dengue
summary: Dengue is common in Sri Lanka. Prevent bites, and know when a fever needs a blood test.
body: Remove standing water around your home every week: flower pots, coconut shells, tyres, blocked gutters and water tanks. Use bed nets for daytime naps, as dengue mosquitoes bite during the day.
If your child has a fever, give paracetamol in the right dose for their weight and plenty of fluids. Do not give ibuprofen or aspirin unless a doctor prescribes it.
A fever lasting more than a day or two should be checked, and your doctor may ask for a full blood count (FBC).
Go to hospital at once if your child has tummy pain, keeps vomiting, bleeds from the gums or nose, is unusually sleepy or passes very little urine. These signs can appear as the fever comes down.

title: Diarrhoea in children: ORS and when to worry
summary: Most tummy bugs pass in a few days. The main job is to prevent dehydration.
body: Give oral rehydration solution (such as Jeevani) in small, frequent sips after each loose stool. Mix it exactly as the packet says.
Keep breastfeeding and keep offering normal food. Your doctor may also give zinc, which helps children recover faster.
Signs of dehydration include fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth, no tears when crying, sunken eyes and unusual sleepiness.
See a doctor urgently if your child shows signs of dehydration, has blood in the stool, cannot keep fluids down or is under six months old.

title: Looking after your mind during pregnancy
summary: Mood swings are common, but feeling low most days is not something you have to push through alone.
body: Hormones, tiredness and worry can make your emotions change quickly in pregnancy. That is normal.

If you feel sad, anxious or empty most days for two weeks or more, lose interest in things you enjoyed, or find it hard to cope, you may have antenatal depression or anxiety. It is common and it can be treated.
Talk to your PHM, your clinic doctor or someone you trust. Rest, short walks, regular meals and time with supportive people all help.
You can call the National Mental Health Helpline on 1926 for free, confidential support. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, seek help immediately.

title: Using your Child Health Development Record
summary: The CHDR book you receive at birth tracks your child's growth, vaccines and milestones. Here is how to make the most of it.
body: Every child in Sri Lanka receives a Child Health Development Record (CHDR). It holds your child's growth charts, vaccination record and development milestones.
Bring it to every clinic and doctor visit. Your PHM will plot weight and height on the growth chart, so you can see whether your child is growing well.
The book lists the national immunisation schedule. Keep every appointment and ask your MOH clinic if you miss one, as most vaccines can still be given.
Read the milestone and feeding pages. If something worries you about your child's growth or development, mention it early.
